home.heading: The student organization for computer science students
home.intro: Beta is the student organization for students in cybersecurity, computer engineering, ICT, or artificial intelligence at UiA Grimstad. The organization is run voluntarily by our students, and the goal is to make everyday student life even better for computer science students.

git.title: Git Workshop
git.introLead: Have you ever wondered how Git actually works, or how to use it like a pro?
git.introRest: In this workshop, {{leadName}}, a 3rd-year AI student, will show you both the basics and the crazy side of version control. He’s been frustrated for a while that the curriculum doesn't teach us this properly, so now he's taking matters into his own hands and sharing skills that will actually save you during projects—both on campus and in your future career.
git.whatYouLearnIntro: Whether you have used Git since kindergarten or never heard of it, you will get a lot out of the workshop. It is aimed at everyone and will cover everything from the basics to the more unusual concepts such as:

topics.1: What Git is and what is actually happening under the hood
topics.2: The most common commands for everyday use
topics.3: Undoing, fixing, and how to change history
topics.4: Practical walkthrough of conflicts and problems
topics.5: Good standards, tips, and tricks for large projects

git.whatToBringTitle: What do I need to bring?
git.whatToBringIntro: The only thing you need is a laptop, so remember to {{installGit}} before Tuesday and make sure you are at least a little familiar with the terminal. Everything will happen without a fancy interface in the terminal so that you actually know what is going on.
git.contact: If you have any questions, contact @jokko4 on {{discordLink}}! See you there!

usage.title: Usage
usage.intro: Using the logo, colors, and icons the right way helps keep things recognizable and professional. That’s why we ask you to always use them correctly by:

items.1: Using the light logo on dark backgrounds and the dark logo on light backgrounds.
items.2: Always keeping logos in their original form, without changing proportions, colors, or content.
items.3: Using the icon when the full logo does not fit, for example as a profile picture, app icon, or on social media.
items.4: Avoiding placing the logo or icon on busy backgrounds that make it harder to read.
items.5: Using the defined profile colors according to the palette below.

verv.title: About roles
verv.heading: About roles
verv.fearTitle: How scary is it to get involved?
verv.fearIntro1: Not at all! As a new board member, you have a 4-week period together with the old board members and you get good experience with all routines and tasks. There are no requirements for previous experience, although it can help, other than that you are engaged in the student community.
verv.fearIntro2: There is room for mistakes and to explore new solutions to problems that may arise. It is also incredibly educational, fun, and valuable to have on your CV. Get involved!!
verv.rolesIntro: At BETA we have a main board consisting of 9 members that you can and should get involved as:

roleDescriptions.leader: is BETA's face towards the faculty, companies, and other associations. The leader ensures that the board is gathered, makes sure the student organization is run well, and that all committees and interest groups cooperate towards the same goal.
roleDescriptions.deputyLeader: is the leader's substitute and is responsible for minutes from board meetings and the student organization's internal structure. The deputy leader is the leader's sparring partner.
roleDescriptions.financeManager: is responsible for BETA's finances. This includes keeping accounts, preparing budgets, and making sure we get paid for company presentations.
roleDescriptions.prManager: is responsible for BETA's profile on various social media platforms; Instagram, Facebook, Discord, and TikTok.
roleDescriptions.betaLanLeader: is responsible for organizing UiA's coolest student LAN every semester.
roleDescriptions.eventCommitteeLeader: is responsible for planning and carrying out social activities for all BETA members.
roleDescriptions.businessCommitteeLeader: is responsible for contact between the business community and the students.
roleDescriptions.betaDevLeader: is responsible for the BetaDEV interest group and the developer community on campus.
roleDescriptions.betaSecLeader: is responsible for the BetaSEC interest group and security-related events.

verv.footer: All committees also have their own deputy leader who is elected internally and does not have a vote in the main board.

intro.title: Introduction
intro.text: Git is a version control system that helps you keep track of code, collaborate with others, and roll back to previous versions if something goes wrong.

howToUse.title: How to use this guide
howToUse.p1: This guide is for beginners who have never used Git, but it also works as a [quick reference](#cheat-sheet) for more experienced users.
howToUse.p2: You can read the guide start-to-finish to learn Git step by step, or use the table of contents as a lookup when you need specific commands.

getStarted.intro1: Before you can use Git, you need to have it installed and configured on your machine.
getStarted.intro2: You can check if you already have Git installed or configured by running these commands in your terminal (or Git Bash on Windows):
getStarted.intro3: If neither command shows anything, or you're unsure, you can follow the next 2 steps.
getStarted.windowsText: You can find the Windows download on [Git's website](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win). This downloads Git Bash, a terminal that gives you Linux-like commands, where you can use Git commands normally.
getStarted.macosText: MacOS requires you to install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) to manage new packages. Once you've done that, you can install Git from the terminal with:
getStarted.linuxText: Linux has many distros with several different package managers. Here is a list of commands to install Git on some popular distros:
getStarted.configIntro: Before you start using Git, you need to tell it who you are and what the name of your first branch is. Your name and email are attached to all the commits you make, making it easier for others to see who did what. Also, most platforms now use the name main instead of master as the default branch.
getStarted.configStep: Set up your name and email (feel free to use your UiA email) and set the default branch to main:
getStarted.configTip: **Tip**: You can use the same email you use on GitHub/GitLab/Gitea so that your commits are linked to your profile.
getStarted.configCheck: You can check that it was configured correctly with:
getStarted.configEditor: If you don't like the editor Git opens by default, you can change it to one of these or whichever editor you prefer:

editorComments.nano: Nano (easy to use in the terminal)

startProject.intro1: When you're ready to start using Git in a project, you have two options:
startProject.opt2: **Clone an existing repository** (from GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, etc.)
startProject.intro2: You can also do a bit of both by initializing a new repository on GitHub or similar, and then cloning an empty project over.
startProject.createIntro1: You can choose to create a Git repository in an existing folder where your project lives, or create a new folder.
startProject.createIntro2: To create a new folder for the project:
startProject.createIntro3: After that, or if you already made the folder and are in it, initialize a new repository with:
startProject.cloneIntro: If you want to work on an existing project from e.g. GitHub, you can clone it over with:
startProject.cloneDesc: This creates a local copy of the entire project with all its history intact. Now you can make changes and send them back with `git push`!
startProject.cloneDiffTitle: **The difference between cloning with HTTPS and SSH:**
startProject.httpsBullet1: Great if you just need to read/copy a repository.
startProject.httpsBullet2: Easy to use with no extra setup.
startProject.httpsBullet3: You have to use a username and password/token when you push changes.
startProject.sshBullet1: More secure and practical in the long run.
startProject.sshBullet2: Uses public/private keys for authentication instead of passwords.
startProject.sshBullet3: Needs to be set up once with `ssh-keygen` and added to GitHub and other services.
startProject.sshTip: **Tip**: If you can, use SSH. If you're just looking around, use HTTPS.
startProject.sshGenerate: Generate SSH key and spam enter
startProject.sshGitHub: Go to GitHub -> Settings -> SSH and GPG keys -> New SSH key, paste the key and give it a name.

workflow.intro: A typical workflow for Git in projects looks like this:
workflow.step2: **Add changes** - choose which changes you want to include.
workflow.step3: **Commit changes** - save a new version with a descriptive message.
workflow.step4: **Push and pull** - share your changes and fetch what others have updated.
workflow.outro: Of course there's more to it, but a lot of your work will look like this.
workflow.statusIntro: To see which files have been changed or are ready to be committed, type:
workflow.statusOutput: If you've made changes to a file, you might get an output that looks like this:
workflow.statusTypes: A file can have 3 different statuses:
workflow.statusUntracked: **Untracked** - Git has no control over the file.
workflow.statusCommited: **Committed** - Git has saved the version of the file.
workflow.addIntro: Before you can commit your changes, you need to tell Git which changes you want to include. This is called "staging" and is done with `git add`. Think of it like packing a box where you carefully choose which items go in before you ship it:

addComments.all: Add all changes in the folder

workflow.addWarning: **Warning**: Be careful with `git add .` - it adds all changed files. Always check with `git status` first!
workflow.resetIntro: You can remove files from the staging area with:
workflow.diffIntro: To see the differences in what you've changed, you can investigate with:
workflow.commitIntro: Once you've added all the changes you want, you can create a commit. It's basically a snapshot of your entire project with the new changes, along with a short message. You do this with `git commit`:
workflow.commitTip: **Tip**: Write commit messages in the imperative mood in English, like "Add user login functionality" or "Fix button styling bug" and commit often. There are also many standards you can agree on; for example, Beta uses [gitmojies](https://gitmoji.dev/) for the website.
workflow.commitCombine: You can also combine add and commit for all tracked files (careful: this includes all changes you've previously run `git add` on):
workflow.pushIntro: To share your changes with others (send them to GitHub, etc.):

pushComments.default: Send to default remote and branch
pushComments.specific: Send to specific remote and branch
pushComments.upstream: Set upstream (where you send it) and push

workflow.pushTip: **Tip**: In GitHub forks, the original repo is often called `upstream` (where changes come from) and your own copy is called `origin`.
workflow.pullTip: **Tip**: Use `git pull --rebase` to avoid unnecessary merge commits.

branching.intro: Branches let you work on different features without affecting the main code or others. It is one of the most important concepts in Git.
branching.tip: **Tip**: Use descriptive branch names with a prefix like `feature/user-auth` or `fix/navbar-placement`.
branching.combineIntro: To merge changes from one branch to another, we use merge (and ideally rebase too):
branching.mergeDesc: When you merge without your branch base being at the top of the branch you are merging into, you'll get an extra merge commit. This is often seen as messy, and it's recommended to use rebase to move your branch to the top before merging.
branching.rebaseTitle: **Rebase** (moves commits to the top of a branch):

rebaseComments.rebase: Rebase feature on top of main

branching.squashIntro: To keep the history clean, it can be useful to combine multiple commits into just one before merging. Although you lose some info, not everyone cares that you made a typo and fixed it on a feature.
branching.squashDesc: Squashing is done through the interface of `git rebase`:
branching.squashInteractive: Interactive rebase of the last 3 commits
branching.squashEdit: In the editor that opens, change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) for the commits you want to combine with the previous one.
branching.squashTip: **Tip**: For a clean history, you should rebase, squash, and then merge so that you can easily read backward through a linear tree.
branching.conflictIntro: When Git can't automatically merge changes, you get one or more conflicts:
branching.conflictDesc: When you open and read the file, all conflicts will be marked like this:
branching.conflictResolve: It's totally up to you how to resolve the conflict, whether you want to keep your own code, the branch's code, or both. Afterwards you need to mark the conflict as resolved and commit the merge:

troubleshooting.intro: Git gives you many ways to undo changes and examine history. Here are a couple of the most used methods and strategies.
troubleshooting.undoIntro: You have several different ways to correct mistakes made during a project:
troubleshooting.undoChanges: **Undo changes**: Revert a file back to the commit's proper version.
troubleshooting.undoCommits: **Undo commits**: Remove the last commit by rewriting history.
troubleshooting.undoWarning: Warning: This rewrites history, so only use it locally!
troubleshooting.revert: **Revert (safer way)**: Undoes a commit by creating an "undo commit" to avoid rewriting history.
troubleshooting.stashIntro: Stash lets you temporarily save changes without committing, which is super useful if you need to make a quick change on another branch or commit but aren't quite finished with your current work:
troubleshooting.stashDesc: The stash structure works like a stack: you place a plate (your changes) on top, and you can do this as many times as you want, but you can only take them back off from the top. This makes stashing very simple and efficient to work with.
troubleshooting.historyIntro: To view the commit history, you can use `git log`. This command can be run in many different ways with different settings so you can see exactly what you want. Here are a few useful versions:
troubleshooting.historyCombine: You can combine them as much as you want like this:

remotes.intro: Remotes are external repositories that you can synchronize with. Usually, `origin` is the main repository on GitHub or other services.
remotes.connectIntro: If you've already cloned a repository, you'll automatically have origin as your default remote. You can check and modify remotes with these commands:
remotes.connectTip: **Tip**: If you are on a fork, it's recommended to add the original repo under the remote name `upstream`.
remotes.connectPush: The first time you push a new branch to the repository, you can create the branch on the remote with:

fetchComments.all: Fetch all changes from all remotes
fetchComments.upstream: Fetch from upstream (if you have a fork)

remotes.fetchTip: **Tip**: Use `git pull --rebase` to avoid unnecessary merge commits.

pushComments.default: Send to default remote and branch
pushComments.specific: Send to specific remote and branch
pushComments.upstream: Set upstream and push new branch

remotes.pushWarning: **Warning**: Never use `git push --force` on shared branches.

standards.intro: To keep projects tidy and make collaboration easier, it's important to follow good standards and conventions. Here are the key practices for structuring Git repositories, commits, and maintaining a professional mindset.
standards.ignoreIntro: The `.gitignore` file tells Git which files and folders should be ignored and not added to version control. This is especially important for avoiding committing sensitive data, build files, and other stuff that doesn't belong in the repository.
standards.ignoreDesc: The file is pretty straightforward to write, and applies to the folder it's in as well as all subfolders. You just write filenames to exclude them, along with a few special characters:
standards.ignoreTip: **Tip**: GitHub has [ready-made .gitignore templates](https://github.com/github/gitignore) for different languages and frameworks that you can copy.
standards.ignoreUndo: If you've already accidentally staged a file, you can remove it again with:
standards.commitIntro: Good commit messages make it much easier to understand what happened in a project and why a change was made. It's super common for students to come back to code they wrote 2 months ago and understand absolutely nothing, or to have to read someone else's code very carefully to figure out what they did.
standards.commitFormat: A smart way to write commit messages is to use a prefix indicating the type of commit, e.g., a fix, feature, documentation, etc. Here's how most people structure their messages:
standards.commitEmojis: There are several ways to write commit messages, and your project group should agree on a style. For this website, we used [gitmojies](https://gitmoji.dev/) so we only need one emoji to communicate the commit's type:
standards.commitTip: **Tip**: Write commit messages in the imperative mood as if you're finishing the sentence "This commit will..." and generally stick to English.
standards.branchIntro: Good branch names make it easy to understand what is being worked on and keep the repository organized.
standards.branchTip: **Tip**: Keep branch names short, use `-` instead of spaces/`_`, and be descriptive yet concise.
standards.contributeIntro: When contributing to someone else's project or working in a team, follow this process to keep things clean:

contributeStep1Comments.fork: Fork the repository first, then clone your fork

standards.contributeStep2: **2. Stay updated with the main repository:**
standards.contributeStep3: **3. Create a new branch for your change:**
standards.contributeTip1: **Tip**: To keep the commit history nice and clean, it's a good idea to run a pull, rebase, and squash before sending it off.
standards.contributeStep6Desc: Go to your fork on GitHub or whatever service you're using, and you'll see a prompt to open a Pull Request (PR) from your branch to the main repo.
standards.contributeTip2: **Tip**: Always read CONTRIBUTING.md and README.md before you start contributing to a project.
standards.repoIntro: A good folder structure makes the project easier to navigate and understand. Usually, all projects also have a standard structure so others can easily contribute to new issues.
standards.repoReadme:
`README.md`:

All introductory info about the project, like the name, how to install it, links to documentation, etc.
standards.repoLicense:
`LICENSE`:

The license dictating how the project can be used and modified.
standards.repoContributing:
`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

How to contribute, naming standards, and everything you need before you start coding away.
standards.repoDocs:
`docs/`:

Folder for project documentation. Often written in markdown, but different projects handle this in vastly different ways.
standards.tagIntro: Tags are used to mark specific versions of your code, which is particularly useful for releases and when you want to refer back to a specific version later. It works similarly to a branch, but it's permanently tied to a commit.
standards.tagTip: **Tip**: Follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/) to make versioning predictable and solid. `Major.Minor.Patch`, bump major for breaking changes, minor for new features, patch for bugfixes.

whatIs.title: What is the general assembly?
whatIs.text: The general assembly is the student association's highest decision-making body and is held every spring semester. This is where we deal with things that matter to the students, elect a new board, and make important decisions for Beta.
whatIs.deadlines: **Deadlines:** starting with the 2027 general assembly, it has to be announced two (2) weeks before the date with a preliminary agenda. Within one (1) week before the general assembly, the full agenda with all the items to be handled has to be published.
whatIs.everyoneVotes: *All members have the right to vote!*

info.title: Important info
info.text1: To keep the general assembly smooth and quick, we've set a deadline for submitting items at least a week in advance. After the deadline we send out all proposals together with an updated agenda, so every student has time to form an opinion on every item. Anything can be brought up, and you can submit as many items as you want.
info.text2: For the student association to keep running, we need everyone interested to run for a position on the board. It's gold for building your CV and has landed many former students both jobs and summer jobs. You learn a lot of new things, get to know loads of new people, and get to shape student life in Grimstad.
info.honoraryMembers: *Honorary members can be proposed as a separate item.*
